confirmed: The source is the seven-page journal version of record, Journal of Creativity 33 (2023) 100066, available online 9 October 2023, with the recorded title and authors (p. 1; PDF page count). The entire markdown, including the references, was read.

The ai_vs_human design and context class and core=no are correct: people and chatbots answered separately, with no randomized AI-assistance study (pp. 2-3, Method). This is an empirical output comparison, not a synthesis (pp. 2-4, Method and Results).

The paper reports 100 human completers, recruited through Prolific, all native English speakers from the USA with full- or part-time work; age M=41.00, SD=12.25, 50 women and 50 men (p. 2, Participants and chatbots). It does not report a count randomized to AI assistance.

Five original chatbots are named, with GPT-4 added after the initial analyses; six human raters are separate from the 100 human creators (pp. 2-3, Participants and chatbots, Procedure, and GPT-4). No-answers and unrelated responses were excluded, and alpa supplied no pants answer (p. 3, Materials).

The five objects were ball, fork, pants, tire, and toothbrush; humans had three minutes per object, with mean study completion time 17 min. Chatbots were asked for more responses up to three times (pp. 2-3, Participants and chatbots and Materials).
Human originality ratings used a 1-5 scale; ICCs were 0.85-0.94, and human-AI rating correlations were rs=0.78-0.94 (p. 3, Procedure and Originality).

The mixed-model results match: human-rated originality B=−0.21, SE=0.15, p=.218; AI-rated originality B=−0.18, SE=0.13, p=.241 (p. 3, Originality). The one-line finding reproduces these results correctly.
Every reported HumanR and AIR mean, SD, t statistic, p value, and Cohen’s d matches its printed row, including the AIR tire and fork rows exactly as printed (p. 4, Table 1).

H > GAI counts in pants, ball, tire, fork, toothbrush order match: HumanR 42, 26, 7, 43, 39; AIR 52, 29, 1, 24, 65. The text reports an across-prompt average of 32.8 humans above the best original chatbot (p. 4, Table 1; p. 3, Originality).

For GPT-4, the paper reports 2, 29, none, 3, and 13 humans above it for pants, ball, tire, fork, and toothbrush, respectively, and an average of 9.4; these follow-up results use AI ratings only (pp. 3-4, GPT-4). The one-line finding reproduces the 9.4 correctly.

The fluency summary reports 2–3 times more ideas from chatbots and originality-fluency correlations rs=−0.28 to 0.26 (p. 4, Fluency). The authors caution that repeated prompting complicates direct fluency comparisons (pp. 5-6, Discussion).

Table S1 and Figs. S1-S4 are referenced as supplementary material; they are not included in the seven-page PDF. The main article supplies the quoted summaries, and supplementary material itself was not read (pp. 3-4, Results; p. 6, Supplementary materials).

No company involvement is reported: affiliations are academic, funding is from the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research, and the authors declare no known competing financial interests (p. 1, affiliations; p. 6, Funding and Declaration of Competing Interest).
summary: The paper correctly belongs to AI-versus-human context evidence: 100 human creators were compared with chatbots, without randomized AI assistance. All reported numerical results match the PDF, but seven corrections are needed to the analysis-unit counts, rating descriptions, and incomplete coding.
